NXS TCS Article — Chapter Analysis

How do the keypaper concepts link across the TCA/Nexus key-sets?

Author

Rainer M. Krug

Published

August 24, 2026

This report examines how the keypaper concepts (the TCA/Nexus definitions) link to one another across the four key-sets — especially the directed link TCA Approaches → TCA Action — and how coherent the keypaper set itself is. It builds toward the combined Approach × Action heatmap at the end.

The heavier corpus-wide analyses (chapter alignment, score distributions, work-type and citation breakdowns) and the cited-literature-embedding “Stage 3” signal have been removed: they depend on the full-corpus embeddings, which are no longer computed in this pruned pipeline.

Keyset linkage

How do the concept definitions link to one another across the four key-sets (the worksheet groups: TCA_Annex_3_3, TCA_Approaches_3_2, TCA_Actions_Ch5, Nexus_Response_Options)? Two directed links are of particular interest — TCA Action → Nexus Response Option and TCA Approaches → TCA Action — each shown below as a set of Sankeys. Two complementary similarity signals drive them:

  • Stage 1 — definition-text similarity (embeddings): cosine similarity between the keypaper definition embeddings (title_abstract, SPECTER2). Two definitions link if their wording/concepts are close.
  • Stage 2 — cited-literature overlap (no embeddings): two definitions link if they cite the same works — Jaccard overlap (Jaccard 1912) of the resolved cited-work sets (only pairs sharing ≥1 work).

Jaccard, P. (1912). The distribution of the flora in the alpine zone. New Phytologist, 11(2), 37–50. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8137.1912.tb05611.x (the “coefficient of community”, defined on p. 39: species common to both / total species in both).

TCA Approaches ↔︎ TCA Actions Ch5

Directed TCA Approaches → TCA Action: for each Approach, its top most-similar Actions under each signal stage.

The Sankeys above only show each Approach’s top matches; the heatmaps below show every Approach × Action pair for both signals. Black borders mark cells scoring above the 95th percentile of that measure’s corpus-wide pairwise distribution — i.e. a stronger link than typical, and unlikely to be chance; unbordered cells are indistinguishable from background.

Combined (Stage 1 + Stage 2, equal weight)

Each cell blends Stage 1 and Stage 2 as equal-weight indicators — each stage’s value expressed as a percentile rank against its own corpus-wide background, then averaged, so neither measure’s raw scale dominates.

Show code 
tar_read(viz_pair_heatmap_appr_act_combined_fig)

*Approach × Action, combined Stage 1 + Stage 2 (equal-weight mean percentile). Center number (large) = the combined score; bottom-left (small) = Stage 1 definition-text cosine similarity; bottom-right (small) = Stage 2 cited-literature Jaccard overlap. Bold marks a value that is itself above its own measure’s 95th percentile (a real link); the center number is bold whenever either component is. Border style (solid = both stages agree, dashed = one stage only, no border = neither) is keyed in the figure’s own “Individual-stage link” legend.

Fill colour and border answer two different questions, and they need not agree. The fill tracks the center number — how unusual this pair is — on ColorBrewer’s colour-blind-safe RdBu palette. Because the combined score averages two percentile ranks taken against the background of all keypaper pairs, white sits at 0.5, meaning “as connected as a typical pair of concept definitions”: red is more connected than typical, blue less. Note this is a relative measure — a Jaccard overlap of 0.03 is tiny in absolute terms but lands high because most concept pairs share no citations at all.

The border answers instead whether an individual stage clears its own 95th percentile, i.e. whether the link is strong enough to be treated as real, and the small bottom numbers are bold on the same test. A cell can therefore be distinctly red yet carry no border — sitting, say, at the 93rd percentile on both stages: high, but short of the significance bar. The colour ranks; the border and bold marks alone certify. The “Jaccard overlap” is Jaccard’s coefficient of community (Jaccard 1912, p. 39; species common to both / total species in both) — the term “Jaccard index” is a later name, not used in the original paper.*
